TextBlock.TextLine: Introduction

The
rocky
headland
known
as
Point
Pinos ,
Monterey
Co.
Cal . ,
re-

ceives
approximately
1.5
million
gallons
of
primarily
treated
sewage

daily .
Adjacent
areas
to
the
sewage
outfall
mouth ,
located
inter-

tidally ,
are
visibly
deficient
in
fauna
and
flora
typical
of
the

rocky
Monterey
coast .

The
purpose
of
this
six
week
investigation
was
to
determine
whether

the
sewage
effluent
affects
the
bacterial
and
diatomaceous
films

known
to
produce
a
substratum
for
the
metamorphosis
of
attached

invertebrate
larvae .
The
importance
of
this
early
film
to
invertebrate

larval
attachment
has
been
debated
for
many .
years .
Most
of
the
previous

microscopic
work
done
on
early
stages
of
invertebrate
settlement
has

been
concerned
with
the
role
of
bacterial
mats
in
fouling
organism

succession
studies .

The
Australian
worker ,
Wood
( 1949 ) ,
in
his
work
on
fouling
organisms ,

suggested
that
bacteria
were
not
necessary
forthe
attachment
of
some

species
of
barnacles
and
other
foulers
to
submerged
surfaces .

ZoBell
and
Allen
( 1935 ) ,
however ,
felt
that
bacterial
and
diatomaceous

slimes
are
not
only
beneficial
to
invertebrate
larval
attachment ,

but
that
for
some
species
this
slime
was
also
mandatory .
An
algal

and
bacterial
film
has
been
shown
by
Hinegardner
( 1969 ) ,
to
be
nec-

essary
for
the
metamorphosis
of
settled
sea
urchins .
Miller ,
Rapean

and
Whedon
( 1943 ) ,
in
their
extensive
review
of
the
importance

of
settlement
surface
preparation
by
bacteria ,
conclude
that
slimes

are
beneficial
but
not
required
for
settlement
of
all
diatom
and

invertebrate
species .

The
recent
preliminary
investigation
of
Golubic
( 1970 ) ,
indicates

the
importance
of
bacteria ,
diatoms ,
cyanophytes
as
an
indicators
of

organic
pollution .
In
his
study
of
nineteen
Yugoslavian
harbors

he
has
found
bacterial - algal
mats
to
persist
throughout
the
year
only

in
the
most
heavily
polluted
areas .
These
mats
consisted
of
a

number
of
species ,
some
of
which
are
directly
dependent
on
water

that
is
rich
in
organic
pollutants .

The
study
described
here
attempts
to
correlate
variations
in

micro - film
formation
with
proximity
to
the
Pacific
Grove
sewage
outfall ..
